name: Where the Counselor's Time Goes
title: Where the Counselor's Time Goes
answer: This idea is that counselors lose too much time to scheduling, paperwork, testing coordination, and routine questions, and AI can take on some of that work. The point is not simply to save time but to return it to students, especially those who are struggling or unsure about their future. If saved time is absorbed by more paperwork, the change helps no one.

sections.body: Counselors often spend hours on tasks that do not need their professional expertise. Scheduling, paperwork, testing coordination, and common questions take time that could go to students. AI can draft routine emails, summarize information for families, or answer common questions through a website helper. The problem this solves is not a shortage of counselor effort but a misdirection of counselor attention. The idea asks schools to make sure any time freed by AI goes back to direct work with students.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a counselor might use AI for routine messages, family summaries, and a website helper for common questions. The text does not divide this by grade band, so the same basic approach applies wherever counselors serve students. Each hour saved is meant to become an hour for meeting with a student who is struggling or unsure about their future. Counselors should track where the saved time goes, following the same tracking approach the book describes for teachers in Chapter 17. Districts can also protect counselor time by removing duties that do not belong to counselors.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no study, figure, finding, or evidence label for this idea. It rests on practice and on the judgment that counselors' time is being used poorly when it goes to routine tasks. The text points to tracking saved time as a practical check, not as a research finding. It also states that time saved but absorbed by more paperwork helps no one. On the evidence question, this idea should be treated as practice-based rather than research-backed.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main risk is that saved time disappears into new paperwork or other duties rather than returning to students. The text says districts should not add new tasks to fill the gap when AI takes over routine communication. Counselors should track where saved time goes so the benefit can be seen and protected. The most valuable counselor work, building relationships and helping students make decisions, cannot be automated and stays with people. The decision about how saved time is used remains a human and district responsibility, not something AI settles.
